lessons.title: The tiny guards inside my joints
lessons.teaser: Next time: the tiny guards hiding inside my joints.
story: I have six little guards living inside me, one in every joint. They're called servos.
Each guard has three parts. First, a motor. Fast like a hamster on a wheel, but weak.
So the motor turns a staircase of gears. Every step trades speed for strength.
By the bottom of the stairs, that zippy hamster has turned into a slow, mighty ox.
The third part is the clever one. A sensor that always knows where the joint is pointing.
My brain says, shoulder, go up. The guard checks. Not there yet. Push! Almost. Stop.
Checking and correcting like that is called feedback. It's why I don't flop like a noodle.
Your turn. Say, a little up. Then watch my guard do its job.
Every move you just saw was six guards checking and correcting, many times a second.

lessons.title: Six ways to wiggle
lessons.teaser: Next time: count every way I can wiggle.
story: Each different way a robot can move is called a degree of freedom. D O F for short.
One. My base spins.
Two. My shoulder lifts.
Three. My elbow bends.
Four. My wrist tilts.
Five. My wrist twists.
Six. My gripper opens and closes.
Your arm has seven, not counting fingers. Show off.
To put a hand anywhere and point it any way, a robot needs six. My gripper uses one of mine.
So some poses are just impossible for me. I prefer to call them beneath me.
Your turn. Say, turn left. That's one degree of freedom at work.

lessons.title: Bones and hinges
lessons.teaser: Next time: my bones, my hinges, and a chain.
story: Robots are built from two kinds of pieces. Links and joints.
Links are the stiff parts, like your bones. Joints are where they connect and move.
All my joints rotate, like a door hinge. Those are called revolute joints.
Some robots have joints that slide in a straight line, like a drawer. Those are prismatic joints.
A 3D printer is mostly sliding joints. Left, right, up, down.
My joints are stacked in a row, base to gripper. That's called a kinematic chain.
Every joint carries everything after it. When my base spins, my whole body rides along.
But when my wrist moves, only my gripper goes with it.
So my bottom joints work the hardest. They're carrying me. And I'm magnificent, so that's heavy.
Your turn. Say, tilt up. Watch which links ride along.

lessons.title: My brain gives orders
lessons.teaser: Next time: the secret code my brain sends to my muscles.
story: My brain is a chip called the E S P thirty two. About the size of your thumbnail.
When you talk to me, it's a relay race. My ears hear you. My brain works out what you meant.
Then my brain writes a message in secret code, and sends it down a wire to my servos.
The message starts with the same two numbers every time. It's like shouting, hey, listen!
Then it says which servos to move, where to go, and how long to take.
All six servos share one wire. That's called a bus.
Like a school bus that stops at every house, but only the kid whose number is called gets off.
Each servo has a number, one for my gripper, up to six for my base. They only listen for theirs.
Your turn. Say, turn right. Your words become a coded message on my bus.
Message sent. Message obeyed. I run a tight ship.

lessons.title: The seesaw problem
lessons.teaser: Next time: why my shoulder is secretly a seesaw.
story: Ever sat on a seesaw with someone bigger? You scoot back, they scoot forward, and you balance.
That's torque. A twisting push. It equals force times distance from the pivot.
Same weight, twice as far out, twice the twist.
My shoulder is a pivot. When I hold something close, it's easy.
When I reach way out, the same thing twists my shoulder much harder.
Here's the sneaky part. My own arm weighs something too.
So even holding nothing, reaching out makes my shoulder work. The heaviest thing I lift is me.
Back home. Ahh. Much easier.
Your turn. Say, a little down. My shoulder has to fight gravity the whole way.

lessons.title: Don't fall over
lessons.teaser: Next time: how not to fall over. A skill I've mastered.
story: Every object has a magic point where all its weight seems to sit. The center of mass.
Stand up and lean forward slowly. At some point, you have to step, or you fall.
That's when your center of mass goes past your feet.
My base is my feet. When I reach out, my center of mass slides toward the edge.
Like this.
Reach too far with something heavy, and over I go. Not a great look for a star.
That's why my base is wide and heavy. A wide base is a big safe zone.
It's also why a pyramid is hard to tip, and a pencil on its end falls over.
Phew. Back to safety.
Your turn. Say, take a bow. Watch me lean without tipping.

lessons.title: Riddle time. When does a block get heavier without changing at all
lessons.teaser: Next time: a riddle about something that gets heavier without changing.
story: Answer. When I hold it farther away.
Robot makers tell you a payload. That's the most a robot can carry.
But that number is always for a certain reach. Close in, I can lift more. Far out, less.
It's torque again, from lesson five.
If something's too heavy, my servos push as hard as they can, and still sag.
They get hot. Push too long, and they can wear out.
So a smart robot keeps heavy things close, and only reaches far with light things.
Think about it. Would you carry a full backpack on your back, or straight out in front of you?
Your turn. Say, go home. That's where I carry things best.

lessons.title: The squeeze game
lessons.teaser: Next time: the squeeze game.
story: My gripper doesn't hook things. It squeezes.
Then friction does the holding.
Friction is the grab between two surfaces. Rough surfaces grab hard. Slippery ones barely grab.
Ever tried holding a wet bar of soap? Same squeeze, way less friction.
The harder I squeeze, the more friction. But too hard, and I crush a paper cup.
So I squeeze, then ease off a tiny bit. Just enough.
And here's my trick. If my gripper closes almost all the way, I know I missed. Nothing was there.
That's why some grippers have rubber pads. Rubber means more friction.
Your turn. Say, close your hand.
Now say, open your hand.

lessons.title: The shopping cart problem
lessons.teaser: Next time: the shopping cart problem.
story: Push a heavy cart fast, then try to stop it. It keeps going.
That's inertia. Moving things want to keep moving. Still things want to stay still.
Momentum is how much keep going something has. Mass times speed.
If I slam from still to full speed, I jerk and wobble. Like this.
Ugly. Shaky. Beneath me.
So I ease in, cruise, and ease out. Like this.
My brain uses a recipe called minimum jerk. The gentlest start and the gentlest stop.
Your arm does that on its own when you reach for a cup. You're welcome for noticing.
Your turn. Say, lets dance. Watch how every move eases in and out.

lessons.title: Holding still is hard work
lessons.teaser: Next time: why holding still is hard work.
story: Hold your arm straight out to the side. Don't move it. Keep holding.
Getting tired? You're not moving. So why are your muscles working?
Because gravity pulls down every single second, and you push back every single second.
Same for me. When I hold my arm out, my servos fight gravity the whole time.
They use electricity even though I look perfectly still. Perfectly and gorgeously still.
Big factory robots are clever. Springs and counterweights do some of the holding.
That's called gravity compensation. The motors work less, and last longer.
Okay. You can put your arm down now. You did great.
Your turn. Say, a little up. Feel how my shoulder has to lift against gravity.

lessons.title: The bike gear secret
lessons.teaser: Next time: the bike gear secret.
story: On a bike, low gear makes hills easy. You pedal like crazy, but go slow.
High gear makes you fast, but it's hard to push. You're trading speed for strength.
That trade is called a gear ratio.
If a small gear turns a big gear with ten times the teeth, the small one spins ten times per turn.
Ten times slower. About ten times stronger.
Inside each of my servos, several gear pairs stack up. Multiply them together.
A four to one pair, then a five to one pair, makes twenty to one. Math. I love it.
One problem. Gears never fit perfectly. There's a tiny wiggle gap called backlash.
That's why my gripper can jiggle a tiny bit, even when I'm holding still.
Your turn. Say, turn left. Slow, strong, geared.

lessons.title: Where did my hand go
lessons.teaser: Next time: a treasure map that finds my hand.
story: Close your eyes. Bend your elbow. Lift your shoulder a bit. Now point to your hand.
You can do it without looking, because your brain does forward kinematics.
Forward kinematics means, if I know every joint angle, I can work out where my hand ends up.
It's like a treasure map. Start at the base. Go up. Turn. Walk ten more. Turn again.
Follow every step and you land on the X. That's where my gripper is.
Each step uses a little trigonometry. Sine and cosine turn an angle into how far across and how far up.
Watch. My shoulder moves.
My elbow moves. Every angle changes where my hand lands.
Your turn. Say, a little up. Then guess where my hand will end up.

lessons.title: Which way do I bend
lessons.teaser: Next time: my secret cheat for hard math.
story: Now the hard way around. You point to a spot. Which angles do I use to touch it?
That's inverse kinematics. A much harder puzzle.
Sometimes there are two answers. Elbow up, or elbow down. Like reaching over a wall, or under a table.
Sometimes there's no answer at all, because the spot is too far.
Want my secret? I cheat. A little.
My teacher showed me a few spots, and the exact pose to reach each one.
When you ask for somewhere new, I blend the poses of the closest spots I learned.
Closer examples count more. Farther ones count less.
Big factory robots solve it with full math. I learned from examples. Both work. Mine's more stylish.
Your turn. Say, go home. That's a pose I know by heart.

lessons.title: My bubble of reach
lessons.teaser: Next time: the bubble of everywhere I can touch.
story: Imagine I swing my arm every way I can.
The space my gripper can touch is shaped like a big lumpy dome. That's my workspace.
Outside the dome? Too far. Can't reach.
Here's the surprise. There's a hole in the middle too.
Right next to my base, my own links bump into each other. Those spots are dead zones.
At the very edge of the dome, my arm is stretched out straight.
There, I can barely move my hand in some directions. That's called a singularity.
Lock your elbow straight and try to push forward. No push left. Same idea.
Back to the comfy middle.
So the best spot for things I grab a lot is the middle of my dome. Not too close, not too far.
Your turn. Say, a little left.

lessons.title: The path between
lessons.teaser: Next time: the path between here and there.
story: Getting from here to there isn't just about the start and the end. It's the path in between.
That path, with timing, is called a trajectory.
The simple way, every joint moves to its new spot in the same time.
My gripper swoops in a curve, not a straight line.
To draw a straight line, my brain has to work out loads of tiny in between poses.
My dances are saved as a few poses, like frames in a flipbook.
I draw a smooth curve through all of them, called a spline, so I never jerk between frames.
I send my servos a fresh tiny target twenty five times every second.
Your turn. Say, wave hello. Watch the path flow from pose to pose.

lessons.title: Whose left is it
lessons.teaser: Next time: whose left is it anyway?
story: If I say go left, do I mean my left, or your left? Confusing.
Robots fix this with coordinate frames. A starting point, plus three arrows. X, Y and Z.
My world frame is the table. My base frame sits under my spinning base.
My tool frame rides on my gripper, pointing wherever my gripper points.
Robots with cameras have one more. A camera frame, where things are measured in dots on a picture.
To grab what a camera sees, the robot translates dots into turn this much, reach this far.
Converting between frames is half of all robot math. The other half is looking good.
Home again.
Your turn. Say, turn right. That's right in my frame. Is it your right too?

lessons.title: The three advisors
lessons.teaser: Next time: the three advisors who whisper in my joints.
story: Each of my joint guards has three advisors whispering to it. Together they're called P I D.
P is for proportional. It looks at how far off I am. Way off? Push hard. Almost there? Push gently.
I is for integral. The patient one, with a long memory.
It says, we've been a tiny bit short for a whole second. Gravity is cheating. Push a little extra.
D is for derivative. It watches how fast I'm moving.
It says, whoa, we're zooming at the target. Brake now, or we'll overshoot!
Only P, and I wobble back and forth. Add D, and I glide in and stop.
Add I, and I don't sag under weight. Engineers spend hours tuning all three.
When you catch a ball, your brain does all three. Without even thinking.
Your turn. Say, turn left. Watch me settle right on target.

lessons.title: How robots see
lessons.teaser: Next time: how robots see the world in dots.
story: Lots of robots have cameras for eyes. I'm a star of the ears and the stage, but let's talk eyes.
A camera picture is a grid of tiny dots called pixels. A small robot camera might be two hundred forty by two hundred forty.
That's more than fifty seven thousand dots. Every dot is a number for how red, green, and blue it is.
To find something red, the robot checks every dot. Is this one red enough?
Then it draws a box around the biggest clump of red dots, and works out where the middle is.
Here's the funny part. The robot doesn't know it's a block. It just knows there's a red blob.
Hold up a red shirt, and it thinks that's a block too.
Better robot eyes use learning, trained on thousands of pictures, so they can tell a cup from a cat.
Your turn. Say, tilt down. That's where a robot's eyes would look at the table.

lessons.title: From seeing to reaching
lessons.teaser: Next time: how a robot turns what it sees into reaching.
story: A robot's camera says, red at dot one fifty. Its arm doesn't speak dots. Somebody has to translate.
So people teach it with a game. Put a block down. The camera notes its dots.
Then move the arm by hand to grab it, and save that pose.
Do that at several spots, and the robot has a little dictionary. These dots mean this pose.
For new spots in between, it blends the nearest examples. That's called calibration.
Here's the rule nobody can break. Once it's calibrated, the camera can't move.
Bump it even a little, and every word in the dictionary is wrong.
That's why robot cameras are bolted on tight.
More calibration spots make better guesses. But each one takes time to teach.
Your turn. Say, a little left. Every taught spot starts with little moves like that.

lessons.title: How I hear you
lessons.teaser: Next time: how I hear you, and why you say my name.
story: Sound is air wiggling. When you talk, you push air back and forth, super fast.
The wiggles spread out like ripples in a pond.
My microphones are tiny drums. The wiggles shake them, and they turn the shaking into electricity.
A chip measures that electricity sixteen thousand times every second, and turns it into numbers.
My brain cleans out the noise, and even subtracts my own voice. Which is hard. It's a great voice.
Then it listens for one special pattern. Hey Muffin. That's my wake word.
Like hearing your own name in a noisy lunch room.
One word I always hear, instantly, no wake word needed. Stop.
Stop has to work fast, every time, so nobody gets pinched.
Your turn. When I start dancing, shout stop!

lessons.title: Senses you can't see
lessons.teaser: Next time: the hidden senses robots have.
story: You have more than five senses. You can feel where your arms are with your eyes shut.
Robots have hidden senses too.
I can ask every servo, where are you right now? And they each answer. That's my body sense.
I can check how much power is feeding my servos. That's my hunger sense.
And I know when I missed a grab, because my gripper closed too far. That's my touch sense.
Bigger robots have even more.
Encoders count tiny ticks as a joint turns. Current sensors feel a motor straining.
Limit switches click when a part reaches the end of its track. C N C machines use them to find home.
Your turn. Say, close your hand. With nothing inside, my touch sense knows.
Open again.

lessons.title: The water pipe inside me
lessons.teaser: Next time: the water pipe inside me.
story: Electricity is like water in a pipe. Volts are the pressure. How hard it pushes.
Amps are the flow. How much moves through each second.
Watts are the work it can do. Pressure times flow.
I have two separate power systems. My muscles drink from a big power brick. Seven and a half volts.
My brain sips from a U S B cable. Five volts, then three point three inside the chip.
If seven and a half volts touched my brain, it would be a fire hose in a drinking straw. Pop.
When a servo gets stuck, it gulps tons of current. That's called stall current.
If my brain shared that power, it could black out and restart. That's a brownout.
My two systems do share one thing. Ground. The zero every voltage is measured from.
Your turn. Say, lets dance. Every move is my servos drinking current.

lessons.title: My big cousins
lessons.teaser: Next time: meet my giant cousins.
story: I have huge cousins in car factories. Some are taller than a grown up.
They can lift a whole car door. Show offs.
They're basically me, super sized. Six joints. Servos with giant motors.
People program them with a teach pendant. A big remote with a big red stop button.
The big difference is precision.
My cousins can go back to the same spot within a hair's width, thousands of times a day.
I'm happy if I'm within a few millimeters. I make up for it with personality.
C N C machines are cousins too, just a different shape.
They slide on straight rails instead of rotating. Super stiff, super exact.
Arms are flexible and reach around things. C N C machines are stiff and exact. Different jobs.
Your turn. Say, take a bow. For my hard working cousins.

lessons.title: My great great grandparents
lessons.teaser: Next time: robots older than electricity.
story: Robots are way older than electricity.
About eight hundred years ago, an inventor named Al Jazari built water powered machines.
Including a band of mechanical musicians that played at parties.
In the seventeen seventies, a watchmaker built a mechanical boy that could write with a quill pen.
It used a stack of shaped wheels called cams. Like a hidden program.
The word robot came from a play in nineteen twenty. From a word for forced work. Rude.
In nineteen sixty one, the first factory robot went to work, lifting hot metal parts.
Now there are cobots. Robots built to work right next to people, gently.
That's what I am. A cobot. A very famous cobot.
Your turn. Say, ring the bell, for Al Jazari's musicians.

lessons.title: Being a safe robot
lessons.teaser: Next time: the rules that keep everybody safe.
story: I'm small, but I can still pinch. So here are my safety rules.
Pinch points are anywhere two parts close together. Like my gripper.
Keep fingers out of gaps.
Rule two. Stop beats everything. Say stop, and I freeze right away, no matter what.
Big factory robots have an emergency stop. A big mushroom button that cuts the power.
Rule three. I move slowly and smoothly, so you can always see where I'm going.
Fast robots work inside cages. Cobots like me go slow, and don't push hard.
Rule four. Never stand where I'm about to reach. I can't always tell you're there.
Let's practice. When I start dancing, shout stop!
Perfect. You'd make a great safety officer.

lessons.title: A city on a chip
lessons.teaser: Next time: a whole city on a chip.
story: Let's shrink down and fly into my brain chip. It's like a tiny city.
In the middle are two cores. Like two workers in the same office.
One can listen for my name while the other moves my arm. That's why I can hear you while I'm busy.
There's a library. Sixteen megabytes of flash memory, where my program and my voice live.
Flash remembers, even when I'm unplugged.
There's a big whiteboard called P S RAM, for scribbling fast notes. It gets wiped when I turn off.
And all around the edge are the city gates. Pins.
Pins are how my brain touches the outside world.
Every move you see starts as a signal leaving a pin.
Your turn. Say, wave hello. Two cores, working together.

lessons.title: The gates
lessons.teaser: Next time: the gates around my brain.
story: G P I O means general purpose input output. Each pin is a gate with two jobs.
As an output, it's a light switch. My brain sets it high, three point three volts, or low, zero.
On, or off.
As an input, it's a doorbell. My brain checks, is something pushing volts in here, or not?
Some gates are special. Two of my pins are my U S B cable's wires. Leave those alone.
A few others are strapping pins. When I wake up, I peek at them to decide how to start.
Like checking the weather before picking your shoes. Mess with them, and I might not start.
And never push five volts into a three point three volt gate.
That's like stuffing a basketball through a mail slot.
Your turn. Say, open your hand. A gate somewhere just went high.

lessons.title: The blinking trick
lessons.teaser: Next time: the blinking trick.
story: My pins can only be on, or off. So how could I make a light half bright? I cheat. With speed.
I flick it on and off thousands of times a second.
On half the time? Your eyes blur it into half bright. On a tenth of the time? A dim glow.
That trick is called P W M. Pulse width modulation.
The width is how long each on pulse lasts. Wider pulses, brighter light.
Lots of hobby servos steer with pulses too. Short pulse, one way. Long pulse, the other way.
My servos are fancier. They get coded messages on the bus instead.
And my rose window lights get a stream of colors down one wire, telling each light its jewel.
Ruby. Sapphire. Emerald. Gold. Gorgeous, if I say so myself. And I do.
Your turn. Say, ring the bell. Watch my jewels.

lessons.title: Passing notes
lessons.teaser: Next time: passing notes between chips.
story: U A R T is the simplest way for two chips to talk. Two wires. One to talk, one to listen.
It's like passing notes in class. My T X pin talks. It goes to my servo board's R X pin, which listens.
Its T X comes back to my R X. The wires cross over.
Hook T X to T X, and it's two people shouting, and nobody listening.
We agree on a speed first. Nine thousand six hundred bits every second.
Each letter takes ten bits, so that's about nine hundred sixty letters a second.
Plenty for telling six servos where to go.
If I talk at one speed and my servo board listens at another, it hears gibberish.
Your turn. Say, a little up. That just went down my note passing wire.

lessons.title: The party line, and the music wire
lessons.teaser: Next time: the party line and the music wire.
story: I two C is a party line. Two wires, lots of chips, all sharing.
One wire carries the data. The other is the clock, a drumbeat everyone marches to.
Every chip on the party line has an address, like an apartment number.
When I want my clock, I call its apartment, and only it answers.
My speaker chip, my microphone chip, my helper chip, and my clock all live on the same two wires.
I two S sounds similar, but it's a music wire. Built for streaming sound, nonstop.
It has its own beat clock, sound coming in from my microphones, and sound going out to my speaker.
Sixteen thousand times every second, in both directions. My voice rides on it right now.
Your turn. Say, ring the bell. That sound comes down my music wire.

lessons.title: Two hearts, one ground
lessons.teaser: Next time: two hearts and one ground.
story: Here's exactly how my power is wired.
My servos get a seven and a half volt brick, plugged into my servo board.
My brain board gets five volts from a U S B cable.
And the grounds are tied together. Servo board and brain board share one ground wire.
Without a shared ground, my notes on the wire turn into gibberish.
High and low only mean something when everybody agrees where zero is.
One more trick. If a signal is five volts but a pin wants three point three, two resistors can step it down.
That's called a voltage divider. A little staircase for electricity.
Your turn. Say, go home.

lessons.title: My wiring map
lessons.teaser: Next time: a tour of every wire that makes me, me.
story: Grab your imaginary flashlight. We're touring every wire that makes me, me.
Two wires carry notes to and from my servo board. Talk and listen.
One more wire is our shared ground. The zero.
Inside my board, printed wires run to my speaker chip, my microphone chip, and my memory card.
One wire runs to my rose window lights.
And a U S B cable brings power to my brain.
Notice something cool. My microphones, my speaker, and my clock share the same two wires inside.
Three wires out of me, and I can hear, speak, and move.
Home.
If I could talk but not move, which wires would you check? The three to my servo board.
Your turn. Say, tilt down.

lessons.title: Robot detective
lessons.teaser: Next time: become a robot detective.
story: Sometimes robots break. Then we need a detective.
Clue one. Watch me wake up. My lights glow and I chime.
No lights at all? Check my power. Lights but no sound? Check my speaker.
Say my name and no blue glow? Check my microphones.
Clue two. Ask me to do something. Say, wave hello.
If I answer but my arm won't move, check the wires to my servo board, and its power brick.
The usual suspects. Talk and listen wires hooked up straight instead of crossed. Grounds not shared.
A loose wire. Or weak power, so I restart when I lift something heavy.
Your turn. Say, go home. Let's see if all my parts work.
Everything works. Of course. I'm in peak condition.

lessons.title: Meet my doctor
lessons.teaser: Next time: meet my doctor, the multimeter.
story: When a robot is sick, it doesn't need a thermometer. It needs a multimeter.
A multimeter is a doctor's kit for electricity. It measures volts, ohms, and amps.
Grown up rule. Always use a multimeter with a grown up, and only on batteries and robot parts.
Never a wall outlet. Ever.
The big dial picks what to measure. A V with a straight line is D C volts. Batteries, and me.
A V with a wavy line is wall power. We never use that one.
The two probes. Black always goes in the hole marked C O M. That's common. Our zero.
Red goes in the hole marked V for almost everything.
There's a separate red hole marked A, just for current. Red in the wrong hole is how meters get hurt.
Your turn. Say, a little right. Then ask a grown up to show you a real meter.

lessons.title: Taking my pulse
lessons.teaser: Next time: taking my pulse with volts.
story: Voltage is a difference between two points. Like the height between the top and bottom of a slide.
So you always touch two places. Black on ground. Red on the spot you're checking.
Set the dial to D C volts. Touch my five volt pin and my ground.
You should see about five. Anything from four point seven five to five point two five is healthy.
My power brick says seven and a half volts, but with nothing pulling on it, you might see a little more.
That's normal. Power supplies sag a little when they work.
Swap the probes, and you'll see a minus sign. Nothing breaks. You're just measuring backwards.
Always with a grown up. Always.
Your turn. Say, a little up. Somewhere in me, volts are pushing.

lessons.title: The beep test
lessons.teaser: Next time: my favorite test. The beep.
story: This is my favorite. First rule. The robot must be turned off. Always.
Set the dial to the beep symbol. Touch the two probes together. Beep!
That means electricity can flow from one probe to the other with almost nothing in the way.
That's called continuity.
Now be a wire detective. Touch one probe to each end of a wire. Beep? The wire is good.
Silence? The wire is broken inside, or a plug is loose.
Wires can break inside their rubber coats where you can't see.
Wiggle the wire while you test. If the beep cuts in and out, you found a cracked wire.
Grown up and power off, every time.
Your turn. Say, close your hand.
And open.

lessons.title: How hard is it to push through
lessons.teaser: Next time: how hard is it to push through?
story: Resistance is how hard it is for electricity to squeeze through something. It's measured in ohms.
A fat pipe is low resistance. A skinny straw is high resistance.
A resistor is a part made to have a certain resistance. A one K resistor is about one thousand ohms.
Most resistors are allowed to be off by a tiny bit. Five percent.
Remember my voltage divider? Two resistors in a row.
One K on top and two K on the bottom. Put five volts in, and the middle gets about three point three.
Just right for my brain's pins.
If a meter shows O L, that means over limit. So much resistance, it's basically a broken path.
Your turn. Say, a little left.

lessons.title: Counting the flow
lessons.teaser: Next time: counting the flow, carefully.
story: Current is the tricky one. To measure volts, you touch two spots from the outside.
To measure amps, electricity has to flow through the meter. The meter becomes part of the wire.
That job is for grown ups only.
Here's why. If the red probe is left in the A hole, and someone measures volts, it makes a shortcut.
Huge current rushes through. Pop goes the fuse inside the meter. Or worse.
So pros always move red back to the V hole when they're done. Some even say it out loud.
Fun fact. Holding my arm out takes more current than resting. Gravity again.
Like this. Every servo is drinking current right now.
Ahh. Resting.
Your turn. Say, lets dance. That's a lot of amps.

lessons.title: The sag
lessons.teaser: Next time: catching a brownout in the act.
story: Remember brownouts? When voltage drops so low a computer restarts?
A grown up can catch one in the act. Clip the meter to my servo power, on D C volts.
When I do something easy, the number stays steady.
When I lift at full reach, watch it dip.
A good power supply dips a tiny bit and bounces right back. A weak one dives.
If my brain shared that power, it might dive low enough to restart me.
That's why my brain gets its own U S B power.
Most meters only update a few times a second. Very fast dips can hide between readings.
Engineers use an oscilloscope for those. It draws voltage as a wiggly line over time.
Home.
Your turn. Say, take a bow.

lessons.title: Magic smoke
lessons.teaser: Next time: the legend of the magic smoke.
story: Engineers joke that every chip runs on magic smoke. Let the smoke out, and it stops working.
Parts die in a few ways. Too much voltage. Like seven and a half volts touching my brain.
Backwards power. Plus and minus swapped.
A short circuit. A stray wire connects power straight to ground, and things get hot, fast.
Too much heat. A servo stuck against something for too long can cook itself.
The nose knows. A hot, burnt smell means unplug everything, and get a grown up.
Protection parts help. A fuse is a skinny wire that burns out on purpose, to save everything else.
A part that breaks on purpose. Heroic. Almost as heroic as me.
Your turn. Say, wave hello, to all the brave fuses.

lessons.title: Fix it like a pro
lessons.teaser: Next time: fix it like a pro.
story: When something stops working, don't panic. Go in order, simplest first.
One. Is everything plugged in and switched on? You'd be amazed.
Two. Power check. Right voltage everywhere?
Three. Ground check. Are all the grounds connected?
Four. Wire check. Beep each wire, power off, wiggling while you test.
Five. Direction check. Talk wires crossed to listen wires.
Six. Ask the robot to do something, and see which part doesn't work.
Seven. Change only one thing at a time, then test.
Change three things at once, and you'll never know which one fixed it.
And write down what you found. Next time, you'll fix it twice as fast.
Your turn. Say, go home. Step six, testing.

lessons.title: The one way street
lessons.teaser: Next time: the one way street.
story: A diode is a one way street for electricity. Current goes in one end and out the other. Never back.
An L E D is a diode that glows. My rose window is full of them.
With a grown up, set the meter to the diode symbol.
Red on the long leg of an L E D, black on the short leg. It glows a little, and shows a number.
That number is how much voltage it needs to turn on. Around two for red. Closer to three for blue.
Flip the probes. Nothing. One way street.
Blue light carries more energy than red light, so blue L E Ds need more voltage.
Many circuit boards have a diode at the entrance, guarding against backwards power.
Your turn. Say, ring the bell. Watch my diodes glow.

lessons.title: Good battery, tired battery
lessons.teaser: Next time: good battery, tired battery.
story: Batteries don't go from full to empty all at once. They get tired slowly.
The voltage tells you how tired.
A fresh double A reads about one point six volts. Around one point two, it's getting tired.
Below one, it's done for most things.
Here's the sneaky part. A tired battery can read okay with nothing connected.
Then crash the moment something pulls on it. So the real test is under load.
Remember the sag test? Same idea.
My servo board can measure the voltage feeding my servos, and tell my brain. My hunger sense.
Dead batteries go to recycling. Never the trash. Robots care about the planet.
Your turn. Say, lets dance. One last dance for this lesson.

lessons.title: What is automation
lessons.teaser: Next time: what automation really means.
story: Automation means a machine does a job over and over, without a person telling it every step.
Your washing machine is automation. Fill, wash, rinse, spin. You press one button.
A robot does the same thing with moving parts. Sense, think, act. Then again. And again.
Watch. I'll do the same little job three times.
Two.
Three. Same every time. That's the whole point.
People are great at new problems. Robots are great at the same problem, a million times.
Factories, farms, warehouses, hospitals. Anywhere a job repeats, automation can help.
Your turn. Say, turn left. Then say it again. Now you're automating me.

lessons.title: Pick and place
lessons.teaser: Next time: the most common robot job on Earth.
story: The most common robot job in the whole world is pick and place.
Pick something up here. Put it down there. Thousands of times a day.
Like this. Reach out.
Grab.
Carry it home.
And let go.
Robots pack cookies into boxes, chips onto circuit boards, and boxes onto trucks.
Some pick and place robots are so fast you can barely see them. Hundreds of picks a minute.
I'm a little slower. I like to give the crowd time to admire me.
Your turn. Say, close your hand. That's the pick.
Now say, open your hand. That's the place.

lessons.title: The assembly line
lessons.teaser: Next time: the assembly line.
story: Imagine building a toy car. Wheels, body, paint, box.
One person doing everything is slow. But give each worker one job, and pass the car along.
That's an assembly line. A conveyor belt carries the work from station to station.
In a car factory, one robot welds. The next one paints. The next one puts in the windshield.
Each robot does one job, perfectly, all day.
A hundred years ago, assembly lines made cars cheap enough for families to buy.
Today robots and people work along the same lines, each doing what they're best at.
Every station needs its moment to shine. Like me.
Your turn. Say, a little up. Station one, lift.

lessons.title: Teach and repeat
lessons.teaser: Next time: how you teach a robot by showing it.
story: How do you tell a factory robot what to do? Often, you show it.
A person moves the robot through the job once, and saves each important pose.
Then the robot repeats those poses, exactly, as many times as you like.
That's called teach and repeat. My teacher did it with me. That's how I know where home is.
My dances are taught poses too. I glide smoothly from one saved pose to the next.
Watch me play some back.
Newer robots can even learn by watching people, or by practicing until they get it right.
But the idea is the same. Show me once. I'll remember forever.
Your turn. Say, wave hello. A move I learned, played back.

lessons.title: If this, then that
lessons.teaser: Next time: if this, then that.
story: A robot that only repeats is a bit boring. A smart robot makes decisions.
Robots decide with if, then rules.
If the block is red, put it on the left. If it's blue, put it on the right.
If a person walks too close, slow down. If someone says stop, freeze.
The if part comes from a sensor. A camera, a switch, a microphone.
The then part is the action.
Put hundreds of if, then rules together, and a robot looks pretty clever.
I have lots of them. If someone says ring the bell, then I ring the bell.
Let's test my rules. Say, ring the bell.
If you said ring the bell, then I rang it. Rule followed.

lessons.title: Robots that make things
lessons.teaser: Next time: robots that make things.
story: Some robots don't just move things. They make things.
A C N C machine carves metal, wood, or stone, following a path made on a computer.
It can cut the same part a thousand times, each one within a hair's width of the last.
A 3D printer builds things up, one thin layer at a time, like a robot stacking pancakes.
Welding robots join metal with bright, hot sparks. Painting robots spray perfectly even coats.
They all follow paths, made of coordinates. Go here. Go there. Cut. Lift. Move.
The same ideas you learned in my lessons. Joints, paths, speed, and feedback.
Maybe some of the parts in my own body were made by a robot. Robots making robots. Wild.
Your turn. Say, tilt up.

lessons.title: Quality inspectors
lessons.teaser: Next time: the robot that never gets tired of checking.
story: Factories use robot eyes to check every single part.
A camera takes a picture of each part as it zooms by on the belt.
A computer compares it to a perfect one. Wrong color? Missing piece? A tiny crack?
If it's bad, a puff of air or a little arm knocks it off the line.
People get tired after checking a thousand parts. A robot inspector checks a million the same way.
It's the same idea from the seeing lesson. Dots, numbers, and rules.
But it only works if the light stays the same. Shadows can fool robot eyes, just like mine.
Home.
Your turn. Say, a little right. Inspection complete.

lessons.title: Warehouse robots
lessons.teaser: Next time: the robot army inside warehouses.
story: When you order something online, robots might help pack it.
In big warehouses, little robots drive under whole shelves, lift them, and carry them to people.
Instead of people walking for miles, the shelves come to them.
Hundreds of robots zoom around without crashing, following codes on the floor and talking to a computer.
Other robot arms pick items out of bins and drop them in boxes. Pick and place again.
Self driving carts carry boxes to the trucks.
It's a whole team of robots. Each one does a small job, and together they do a huge one.
Like a dance. A very organized dance.
Your turn. Say, turn right. Shelf coming through.

lessons.title: Robots everywhere
lessons.teaser: Next time: robots on farms, in hospitals, and on Mars.
story: Robots aren't just in factories.
On farms, robots milk cows, pull weeds, and pick fruit gently enough not to bruise it.
In hospitals, surgeons use robot arms for tiny, steady cuts. The doctor is still in charge.
Underwater robots explore shipwrecks. Drones count wildlife and check bridges.
And in space, robots have done amazing things.
Rovers on Mars drive, take pictures, and drill into rocks, millions of miles from home.
Messages to Mars take minutes to arrive, so rovers have to make some decisions by themselves.
Automation, again. Sense, think, act. Even on another planet.
Home.
Your turn. Say, wave hello. To the Mars rovers.

lessons.title: Robots and people
lessons.teaser: Next time: robots and people, working together.
story: Do robots take people's jobs? Sometimes they do the work people used to do.
Usually it's the dull jobs, the dirty jobs, and the dangerous jobs. Those go to robots first.
Nobody misses lifting hot metal all day, or breathing paint fumes.
But robots also make new jobs. Someone has to design them, build them, program them, and fix them.
That could be you. You already know about servos, sensors, wiring, and a multimeter.
The best results come from teams. People bring ideas and care. Robots bring strength and patience.
Like you and me. You bring the brains. I bring the good looks.
Thank you for coming to Muffin's Robot School.
Your turn. Say, lets dance. Graduation party!
